title: Together.ai: Prompt Leakage for Requests
content:
We are notifying customers about a security incident involving a subset of prompts submitted to Together AI’s serverless inference service in June and July 2026. An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after a credential for a private repository was exposed in a public code repository.
We apologize for this incident. We are reviewing the affected data to determine what information was exposed and which customers require direct notification.
What happened
As part of routine software testing, we collected prompt samples authorized for that use and stored them in a private Hugging Face repository. The samples came from requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.
During development of our public GitHub repository, xorl, an AI coding agent committed a credential that provided access to the private Hugging Face repository. Our automated scanning detected the exposed credential, and we reverted the commit.
During the exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored prompt samples. The party subsequently searched those samples for credentials to other services and tested whether those credentials were valid. Five of the credentials tested were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment.
Investigation and scope
We have worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement to investigate the incident.
Based on our review, we have not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident. Our review of the affected prompt contents is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed. We will contact affected customers directly as needed with the findings relevant to them.
Changes we have made
Following the incident, we strengthened controls around development workflows, credentials, and customer data. These changes include:
- Using scoped or short-lived credentials, and keyless access where supported, to reduce the potential impact of credential exposure.
- Checking all pull requests for credentials.
- Making zero data retention (ZDR) the default setting for new accounts.
- Updating our development processes governing the use of AI coding agents.
What customers can do
Customers handling sensitive prompt data should enable ZDR in their account settings.
If you have questions about this incident or its potential impact on your organization, contact security@together.ai.
Vipul Ved Prakash
CEO and Co-founder, Together AI

report.summary: An AI coding agent leaked a credential to a public GitHub repo, letting an outsider download stored prompt samples from Together AI's serverless inference service.
report.background: Prompts sent to hosted inference APIs are frequently logged for debugging, quality evaluation, and abuse monitoring — which means they sit in storage as plaintext that may contain proprietary business logic, customer data, or even API keys pasted in by users. Together AI's incident sits at the intersection of two converging risks: the sprawl of long-lived cloud credentials across development tooling, and the rapid adoption of autonomous AI coding agents that can commit files, run scripts, and touch repositories with limited human oversight. The company stored authorized test samples in a private Hugging Face repository — a common pattern now that Hugging Face hosts datasets as well as models. Meanwhile, zero data retention (ZDR) has become a competitive differentiator for enterprise-grade inference providers, and buyers increasingly demand it contractually. The incident also shows how quickly a single exposed secret can be weaponized: the attacker did not stop at reading prompts, but mined them for downstream credentials, a technique that turns one leak into a cascading breach.
key_points: The root cause was a credential, not a model flaw. An AI coding agent working on Together AI's public GitHub repository 'xorl' committed a secret that unlocked a private Hugging Face repo holding stored prompt samples. Automated scanning caught it and the commit was reverted, but the window was enough for an outside party to copy the data.

The exposed prompts came from specific models and dates. Samples originated from requests to MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6, concentrated on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026 — roughly a month of testing data rather than the full production firehose.

The attacker went credential-hunting inside the prompts. After downloading the samples, the party searched them for keys to other services and tested whether those keys worked. Five turned out to be canary credentials from a Dragos security experiment — a strong signal that some prompts contained live-looking secrets.

Forensics found no second leak, but content review is unfinished. Together AI is working with an external forensics firm and law enforcement, and says it has not found evidence of additional prompt leakage. It is still reviewing prompt contents for personal or sensitive data and will notify affected customers individually.

Remediation centers on shrinking secret blast radius. The company is moving to scoped or short-lived credentials and keyless access, scanning every pull request for secrets, making zero data retention the default for new accounts, and rewriting rules for how AI coding agents touch its development workflow.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the episode reframes model providers as data custodians: the sensitive asset is not just weights but the prompts flowing through them, which often contain more business value than the model output. Expect enterprise buyers to push harder on ZDR, contractual prompt-confidentiality clauses, and audit evidence for how vendors isolate test data. For developers, the lesson is that AI coding agents must be treated as untrusted contributors — sandboxed, denied ambient credentials, and gated by push protection rather than post-hoc scanning. Any key that touches an LLM prompt should be assumed compromised and rotated. For regular users, the practical takeaway is simpler: never paste API keys, passwords, or personal records into a chatbot or API call, because retention policies vary by account tier and logging is often on by default.
report.tools: To reduce similar exposure, adopt secret scanning with push protection (GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks, TruffleHog) and run it as a pre-commit hook, not just in CI. Replace static keys with short-lived or keyless credentials via OIDC federation (HashiCorp Vault, AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, GitHub Actions OIDC). For detecting misuse, deploy canary tokens (Canarytokens.org, Dragos canaries) in repositories and prompts. Check whether your inference provider offers zero data retention, and if you self-host, evaluate vLLM or Ollama with logging disabled for sensitive workloads.
